title: Fuel Smell From Exhaust
summary: Common causes, likely diagnostic paths, OBD references, and repair-next steps for fuel smell from the exhaust.
intro: A fuel smell from the exhaust usually means the engine is running rich, misfiring, or sending unburned fuel into the exhaust stream. The useful split is whether the smell is coming from an active misfire, a leaking injector, or control data that is commanding too much fuel.
common_sounds: Raw fuel smell at idle or after a hot soak
Rough idle or stumble with the odor
Dark exhaust or heavy exhaust smell on acceleration
Fuel economy dropping without another obvious cause
quick_checks: Scan for misfire, O2-sensor, and catalyst-efficiency codes before replacing parts
Inspect spark plugs for fuel fouling or one wet cylinder
Review fuel trims and O2 sensor behavior on scan data
Listen for injector issues and consider whether one cylinder is leaking down
Do not ignore sulfur smell or power loss if catalyst damage may already be developing
common_causes: Active misfire leaving raw fuel in the exhaust
Biased oxygen sensor or rich-running control fault
Incorrect airflow or temperature input causing overfueling
Catalytic converter no longer cleaning up the exhaust stream efficiently
diagnostic_paths: If the fuel smell comes with a clear misfire, start with P030x ignition and injector checks before chasing sensors.
If fuel trims are rich without a strong misfire, compare upstream and downstream O2 data and verify airflow inputs.
If one cylinder plug is wet or heavily fuel-fouled, injector leak-down becomes more important.

diagnostic_path_sections.title: Misfire and Raw Fuel Path
diagnostic_path_sections.summary: When fuel smell comes with a rough run, keep spark and injector checks ahead of catalyst replacement.
checks: Scan misfire counters and inspect the wet or fouled cylinder
Check spark plug, coil output, and injector pulse
Verify compression if the misfire does not follow ignition or fuel parts

diagnostic_path_sections.title: O2 and Catalyst Path
diagnostic_path_sections.summary: When trims or catalyst codes overlap, compare O2 data and exhaust leaks before condemning the converter.
checks: Review upstream and downstream O2 behavior
Inspect exhaust leaks before the catalyst
Check for rich-running causes that can damage the converter

recommended_repairs.title: Oxygen Sensor Blueprint
recommended_repairs.description: Relevant when scan data shows biased sensor behavior or heater issues behind a rich-reading path.

recommended_repairs.title: Fuel Injector Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: A strong next path when one cylinder is wet, rich, or leaking down after the engine sits.

recommended_repairs.title: Spark Plug Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Useful when incomplete combustion and plug fouling are contributing to the raw-fuel smell.

recommended_repairs.title: Ignition Coil Blueprint
recommended_repairs.description: Relevant when weak spark is leaving unburned fuel in the exhaust stream.

recommended_repairs.title: Catalytic Converter Replacement Cost
recommended_repairs.description: Only use this path after upstream misfire or rich-running causes are ruled out or repaired.
